DUNHUANG, IN MOTION

The journeys of
Dunhuang manuscripts.

XIWEN WANG HY5419 · National University of Singapore

Manuscript circulation and scholarship

The Library Cave at Mogao was discovered in 1900. Over the next decade, batches of its contents were acquired and transported to London, Paris and Beijing.

This project examines manuscript circulation and scholarly work between 1900 and 1910. It covers transfers involving Aurel Stein, Paul Pelliot and the Qing government, alongside correspondence, photographs, cataloguing and scholarly exchanges. It also identifies five present-day collecting institutions represented in this case study.

How to read this graph

03 / WHERE THEY ARE NOW

Related collecting institutions

The five institutions shown here are in London, Paris and Beijing. Their manuscript and print collections are listed separately from related paintings and objects. Each entry links to an official collection page.

These institutions represent this case study, not a complete inventory of Dunhuang collections. Locations are city-level references; holding an object does not mean it is on public display.

ABOUT THIS PROJECT

Manuscript circulation and Dunhuang scholarship

The map records transfers between places; the network records the people, institutions and events involved. Select a transport record or scholarly activity to consult its sources before drawing connections between them.

04 / BEHIND THE MAP

Sources and evidence

The route map and relationship network draw on expedition accounts, correspondence, research publications and collection catalogues. Select a map connection or network node to consult its sources and evidence notes. Unverified stops and links to individual manuscripts are left unspecified.

Download exhibition data ↓
01

Routes and locations

Map lines represent geographical connections recorded in the sources, rather than every stop along a journey. Unverified stops, ports and historical buildings are left unlocated. Present-day museum addresses are not used as historical handover sites.

02

Transport and accession records

Pelliot’s main expedition cargo arrived in Paris in 1909; the BnF records entry of the manuscripts into its department in 1910. These are recorded separately. Cases, scrolls, objects, images and catalogue numbers retain their original units and are not converted into one another.

03

Batches and individual manuscripts

Most historical connections are based on records of batches or whole collections. Apart from a few verified catalogue examples, this project has not matched individual manuscripts to every historical handover.
